extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school and undergraduate students (including math-olympiad contestants) studying polynomial theory
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level reference on polynomials: definitions, theorems (division algorithm, factor theorem, Vieta, roots of unity, reciprocal and symmetric polynomials), standard solution techniques and worked examples used in olympiad/contest-style problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial Division Algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: For polynomials f(x), g(x) (g ≠ 0) there exist unique polynomials q(x) and r(x) so that f(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x), with deg r < deg g or r(x) = 0; q(x) and r(x) are quotient and remainder on division of f by g. If r(x)=0, we say g(x) divides f(x) and write g(x) | f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explicit remainder/quotient uniqueness; used throughout to reduce degree, compute remainders, and define divisibility. Example E1 demonstrates polynomial long division producing q(x) and r(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remainder Theorem / Division by x−a
rubrics_metrics.description: Division of f(x) by x−a yields f(x) = (x−a) q(x) + r with r ∈ R; setting x=a gives r = f(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compute remainders quickly and to derive the factor theorem (if f(a)=0 then x−a divides f). Stated in formulas (1) and (2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: f(a) = 0 ⇔ f(x) = (x−a) q(x) for some polynomial q(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollary of the remainder theorem; used to factor polynomials and to build factorizations with multiple distinct roots (e.g., if f has distinct zeros a1,...,an then f(x) = c ∏(x−ai)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of a Root and Derivative Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A has multiplicity m if there exists m ∈ N and polynomial q with f(x) = (x−a)^m q(x) and q(a) ≠ 0. Equivalently, f(a) = f'(a) = ... = f^{(m−1)}(a) = 0 and f^{(m)}(a) ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives both algebraic (factor) definition and analytic criterion via derivatives (stated as equivalence of (4) and (5)); useful to detect and prove multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integer and Rational Root Criterion (Rational Root Theorem specialization)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x)=a_n x^n + ... + a_0 has integer coefficients and z∈Z is a root, then z | a_0. If the leading coefficient a_n = 1 (monic), then every rational root is an integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches provided: substitution and divisibility argument for integer roots; clearing denominators and gcd(p,q)=1 shows q must be 1 for monic polynomials. Use to restrict possible rational roots in searches/trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monic Polynomial Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A polynomial with highest-degree coefficient a_n = 1 is called monic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in statements like the rational-root consequence above and in Vieta relations for simplified coefficient relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vieta's Formulas (Relations between Coefficients and Roots)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quadratic x^2 + p x + q with roots x1,x2: p = −(x1+x2), q = x1 x2. For a cubic x^3 + p x^2 + q x + r with roots x1,x2,x3: p = −(x1+x2+x3), q = x1x2 + x2x3 + x3x1, r = −x1x2x3. Similar relations exist for higher-degree monic polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compute symmetric sums of roots from coefficients and vice versa; applied in examples (E2, etc.) and in solving symmetric systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifted-basis Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A polynomial f(x) of degree n can be written about a point a as f(x) = c_n (x−a)^n + ... + c_1 (x−a) + c_0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by substitution x = a + (x−a). Useful for Taylor-like expansions about a point and handling multiplicities or local behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and Linear Factorization over C
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonconstant complex-coefficient polynomial f(z) = a_n z^n + ... + a_0 (a_n ≠ 0) has at least one root in C. Hence each polynomial of degree n can be written as f(x) = c ∏_{i=1}^n (x − x_i), with x_i ∈ C (not necessarily distinct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational: justifies factoring into linear factors and counting multiplicities; used when discussing complex roots and root-of-unity decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roots of Unity and Cyclotomic Factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ω = e^{2π i / n}. Then x^n − 1 = ∏_{k=0}^{n-1} (x − ω^k). If gcd(k,n)=1, powers ω^k generate all nth roots of unity. For example x^3 − 1 = (x − 1)(x^2 + x + 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reason about divisibility by cyclotomic polynomials, to test when polynomials vanish at roots of unity, and to deduce factorizations and divisibility properties (see E3, E4, E35).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Roots of Unity to Test Divisibility (Evaluation at ω^k)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polynomial F(x) is divisible by a cyclotomic factor (e.g., x^2+x+1), one can test divisibility by evaluating at the relevant roots of unity (ω, ω^2, ...). If F(ω)=0, etc., then the factor divides F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated in multiple exercises: E3 (checking x^2+x+1 | x^{2n}+x^n+1 by evaluating at ω), E4 (setting x to ω^j to derive linear equations), E35 (finding remainder by evaluating at fifth roots). This is a standard technique for divisibility checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardano-style Reduction for Cubics via Roots of Cubic's Decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: For cubic x^3 + p x + q = 0, set x = −a − b and relate p = −3ab, q = a^3 + b^3; then a^3, b^3 are roots of z^2 − q z − p^3 / 27 = 0, giving a^3 = q/2 ± sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27) and analogous formula for b^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the classical cubic solution structure (presented in text around equations (7)-(9)). Useful to derive explicit forms of cubic roots and to reason about discriminant-type expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructibility via Cyclotomic Polynomials (e.g., Regular Pentagon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorizations like x^5 − 1 = (x − 1)(x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1) provide algebraic equations for roots ω; relations among sums of powers yield explicit algebraic expressions for cosines (e.g., cos 72° = (√5 − 1)/4), showing constructibility by ruler and compass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how algebraic factorization leads to classical constructibility results; the chapter demonstrates constructing segment a = cos 72° from polynomial identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial-interpolation/auxiliary-polynomial trick for integer-value constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a polynomial value given constraints at integer points, form an auxiliary polynomial that vanishes at given integers: e.g., in E5 define Q(x) = (x+1)P(x) − x; Q(k)=0 for k=0..n, so Q(x) = a x(x−1)...(x−n); determine a by plugging a special x (like x=−1), then recover P(n+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General method: build polynomial with known zeros to pin down unknown coefficients; essentially Lagrange interpolation / finite-difference idea applied to contest problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: No 3-cycle for integer-coefficient polynomials on distinct integers (E6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P(x) has integer coefficients and a,b,c are three distinct integers, the conditions P(a)=b, P(b)=c, P(c)=a cannot all hold simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses factorization P(x)−b = (x−a)P1(x) etc. and a maximal-difference argument leading to contradiction. This is a criterion to rule out certain cyclical mappings by integer polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal Polynomial Definition and Reduction to Polynomial in z = x + 1/x
rubrics_metrics.description: A polynomial f(x) = a_0 x^{2n} + a_1 x^{2n−1} + ... + a_1 x + a_0 is reciprocal iff a_i = a_{n−i} for i=0,...,n. Any reciprocal polynomial of degree 2n can be written as x^n g(z) where z = x + 1/x and g(z) is a polynomial in z of degree n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an explicit change of variable reducing reciprocal polynomials to polynomials in z; useful for solving reciprocal equations and factoring them by lowering effective degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of Reciprocal Polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) f(x) reciprocal iff x^n f(1/x) = f(x). (b) Every reciprocal polynomial of odd degree is divisible by x+1 and quotient is reciprocal of even degree. (c) If a is a zero, then 1/a is also a zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural properties help factor and analyze reciprocal polynomials and their root sets; useful in E12 and related problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing x^k + 1/x^k as Polynomial in z = x + 1/x
rubrics_metrics.description: There are explicit polynomial relations: x^2 + 1/x^2 = z^2 − 2, x^3 + 1/x^3 = z^3 − 3z, x^4 + 1/x^4 = z^4 − 4z^2 + 2, etc., so x^k + 1/x^k can be written as a polynomial in z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides recurrence/explicit transformations used when reducing reciprocal polynomials or solving equations invariant under x ↦ 1/x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric Polynomials in Two Variables: Representation and Power-sum Recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: A polynomial f(x,y) symmetric (f(x,y)=f(y,x)) can be represented as a polynomial in σ1 = x+y and σ2 = x y. Power sums s_n = x^n + y^n satisfy s_0 = 2, s_1 = σ1, and for n ≥ 2: s_n = σ1 s_{n−1} − σ2 s_{n−2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental tool: reduce symmetric systems to lower-degree equations in σ1,σ2; then solve quadratic z^2 − σ1 z + σ2 = 0 to recover x,y. Illustrated in examples E7–E9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solving Symmetric Nonlinear Systems via Elementary Symmetric Polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: For symmetric systems in two or three variables, substitute σ1,σ2 (and σ3 for three variables) to lower the degree: find σ-values, then recover variables as roots of quadratic/cubic with coefficients σ. For three variables, use cubic u^3 − σ1 u^2 + σ2 u − σ3 = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied repeatedly in exercises E7–E11 and the section 'Symmetric Polynomials'. Yields systematic reduction technique for many contest problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power-sum Identities for Three Variables (expressing s_n via σ1,σ2,σ3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power sums s_i = x^i + y^i + z^i (i=0,1,2,...) can be represented using σ1,σ2,σ3. Examples: s2 = σ1^2 − 2σ2; s3 = σ1^3 − 3σ1σ2 + 3σ3; s4 = σ1^4 − 4σ1^2 σ2 + 2σ2^2 + 4σ1σ3, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides explicit formulas useful to convert symmetric sums appearing in constraints into polynomial relations among σ1,σ2,σ3, after which one solves a cubic to recover variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Value-constraints and Roots to Force Polynomial Identities (many problem techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polynomial of degree ≤ m takes the same value at m+1 distinct points, it is constant equal to that value (used to deduce remainders); similarly, a polynomial with more zeros than its degree must be identically zero. Also, evaluation at specially chosen points (often roots of unity or integers like ±1) is used to determine unknown constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in multiple examples (e.g., proving remainder is constant 5 in E35, deducing Q(x)−c has n roots so is zero in problem about table products). This is a standard toolkit item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digit-sum divisibility trick (for divisibility by 3 in base 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating divisibility of large decimal-represented numbers, the sum-of-digits criterion can show divisibility by 3 (e.g., in E3(b) the digit sum 3 implies divisibility by 3, used in factoring the decimal rep by 3·37).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple number-theory trick used in combination with polynomial/cyclotomic reasoning to deduce divisibility by specific primes (here 3 and 37).

rubrics_metrics.name: General technique: reduction by substitution and factoring (various ad hoc transforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common tactics: set x = a + (x−a) to expand about a; divide by suitable powers (e.g., divide by z^4 in E11) to transform to a reciprocal/standard form; set y = x−a or similar shifts to simplify symmetric expressions; rewrite polynomials by adding/subtracting convenient expressions to reveal factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a compendium-style entry summarizing many ad hoc manipulations used across worked examples and problems; the chapter demonstrates multiple instances (shifts, dividing, multiplying, pairing terms) to reveal structure and factorization.
